Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) is responsible for the conservation and management of migratory birds in Canada. The Migratory Bird Convention Act and the Migratory Birds Regulations, 2022 (hereafter, the Regulations) provide the regulatory framework to enact migratory bird conservation in Canada. The Regulations protect the nests of all migratory birds when they contain a bird or viable egg (i.e., during the nesting period). Activities that result in vegetation clearing during the nesting season are likely to contravene the prohibitions on destroying or disturbing nests laid out in the Regulations, unless these activities are authorized under the authority of a permit.

Incidental take is the inadvertent, yet predictable, killing or harming of migratory birds or the destruction or removal of their nests and eggs during activities that are otherwise conducted legally. There are currently no means (i.e., permit) of lifting the prohibitions laid out in the Regulations for activities that cause incidental take. However, ECCC recognizes the need to provide regulatory certainty to proponents that are conducting activities that may result in incidental take in certain scenarios, in a way that benefits migratory birds. Accordingly, ECCC is committed to developing an incidental take regime and is in the process of evaluating the various factors that are likely to impact the risk of causing incidental take, including the location and timing of the activity with regards to the nesting period.

ECCC created a tool to help predict the periods during which migratory birds are likely to be nesting in a particular geographic area. This tool is used by stakeholders to support project planning and risk-management decisions regarding the impact of their activities on breeding birds. The tool has also been used by NGOs, such as the Nesting Calendar Query Tool currently published by Birds Canada, to inform the public about the breeding periods of migratory birds.

The existing nesting calendars are predictions derived from a set of models developed for studying the nesting phenology of bird species breeding in Canada developed by ECCC biologists (Rousseu and Drolet, 2015) using historical nest-record data (from the NestWatch project; Bird Studies Canada, 2013). The nesting periods for 311 species were modelled, including 264 migratory bird species.

Since the original nesting-calendar models were developed, substantial additional sources of breeding information have become available. These may include recent breeding bird atlas data, eBird observations, point-count information, rare-species forms, and additional nest records from the project NestWatch (> 2013). Many of these datasets contain dated breeding-evidence codes that will provide information about nesting phenology. Additionally, ECCC would need to develop nesting calendars for all 401 migratory bird species currently recognized under the MBCA.

ECCC aims to assess and update the existing nesting calendars for 1) all species Canadian migratory birds individually and 2) for species combined, to identify core breeding periods across Canada’s landscape for all migratory birds to help inform the future incidental take regulatory regime. The updated calendar should incorporate new nest records from all the relevant sources of data identified by ECCC.
